title: My plans: aller + infinitive
why: With aller + infinitive, you can finally talk about the future: what you're going to do tonight, this weekend or next summer. It's the most common way to talk about plans in everyday French, and you already know all the pieces.
json:
{"lessons": ["

Je vais + infinitive: going to

Good news: the most common way to talk about the future in French works exactly like English “going to”. Take aller in the present, which you know well, and add an infinitive.

aller+ infinitiveEnglish
jevaispartirI'm going to leave
tuvaspartiryou're going to leave
il / elle / onvapartirhe / she is, we're going to leave
nousallonspartirwe're going to leave
vousallezpartiryou're going to leave
ils / ellesvontpartirthey're going to leave
Ce soir, je vais dîner avec Léa.Tonight, I'm going to have dinner with Léa.
Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?What are you going to do this weekend?
Mes parents vont visiter la Bretagne en juin.My parents are going to visit Brittany in June.

Now you understand Je vais prendre…, which you used at the café as a fixed phrase: it simply means “I'm going to have…”. You can even say Je vais aller à Lyon: aller + aller is perfectly normal.

Plans in the present

English often uses the -ing form for arrangements: “I'm having dinner with Léa tonight”. French can use the near future or the plain present with a time word: Ce soir, je dîne avec Léa. And for a timetable, French uses the present, like English: Le train part à 8 h (The train leaves at 8), Le film commence à 21 h.

Don't confuse movement and plans: Je vais au marché (I'm going to the market: a place) and Je vais acheter du pain (I'm going to buy bread: a plan). Both use aller, as in English.

", "

Negation, pronouns and pronominal verbs

Since aller is the conjugated verb, the negation goes around it, and the infinitive stays outside:

Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.I'm not going to go out tonight.
Elle ne va pas venir : elle est malade.She isn't going to come: she's sick.
On ne va pas prendre la voiture.We're not going to take the car.

Object pronouns go before the infinitive

As with vouloir and pouvoir, the pronoun belongs to the infinitive and goes right in front of it: Le film ? Je vais le voir demain. Tu vas l'appeler ? Je ne vais pas les attendre.

Pronominal verbs: the pronoun matches the subject

With a pronominal verb, the reflexive pronoun stays in front of the infinitive and changes with the subject. English “I'm going to bed” is Je vais me coucher.

se reposerEnglish
jevais me reposerI'm going to rest
tuvas te reposeryou're going to rest
il / elle / onva se reposerhe / she is, we're going to rest
nousallons nous reposerwe're going to rest
vousallez vous reposeryou're going to rest
ils / ellesvont se reposerthey're going to rest

A very common mistake: je vais se coucher. The pronoun is not part of the infinitive, it follows the person: je vais me coucher, nous allons nous lever tôt.

", "

When? Time markers

To place your plans in time, you need a set of markers. Most of them can go at the start or at the end of the sentence: Demain, je vais travailler or Je vais travailler demain.

FrenchEnglish
ce soirtonight, this evening
ce week-endthis weekend
demain / demain matintomorrow / tomorrow morning
après-demainthe day after tomorrow
lundi prochainnext Monday
la semaine prochainenext week
le mois prochainnext month
l'année prochainenext year
dans deux jours / dans une heurein two days / in an hour (from now)

Take ce soir and ce week-end as fixed markers for now. Prochain is an adjective: it goes after the noun here and agrees with it, le mois prochain, la semaine prochaine.

Dans, not en

To say when something will happen, counting from now, use dans: Je pars dans trois jours (I'm leaving in three days). En + duration means how long something takes: Je fais le trajet en trois heures (I do the trip in three hours). English uses “in” for both, so this is a frequent slip.

On part en vacances dans deux semaines. On va louer une maison à la mer.We're going on vacation in two weeks. We're going to rent a house by the sea.

Planning a trip? Visiter is for places: visiter Lyon, visiter un musée. For people, say voir des amis or aller chez mes parents.
